issues.legal_issue: The statutory term for a building being held at the time of vesting requires lawful holding, not mere physical possession.
material_facts: The statutory scheme provided for estate vesting and deemed settlement of specified buildings with the persons who held them.
The appellants were physically occupying the site and a cow-shed at vesting after unlawfully entering the site and demolishing the respondents’ residential buildings.
The respondents claimed that they had lawfully held the buildings and site before their temporary departure.
issues.conclusion: The term “held” means lawfully held; mere physical possession by a trespasser does not qualify for deemed settlement.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 6 and 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, read in the context of the Act’s scheme and language, “held” in section 9 means lawfully held. This construction accords with justice and reason and with the use of “held” alongside “belonging.” The Court approved Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra, disapproved Bharat v. Ch. Khazan Singh, and applied the interpretive approaches in K.K. Handique v. Member, Board of Agricultural Income-tax, Assam and Eramma v. Verrupanna.

predicates.land_reform_building_settlement_case: The dispute concerns whether a person’s holding of a building qualifies for settlement under a land-reform scheme.
predicates.claimant_had_legal_title_to_building: The claimant had legal title to the building.
predicates.claimant_lawfully_held_building: The claimant held the building lawfully.

issues.definition: When a building-settlement dispute arises under a land-reform scheme, a building qualifies for deemed settlement only if the claimant held it lawfully or had legal title to it.

issues.legal_issue: A lawful holder who temporarily leaves a building without abandoning it may recover the building and site after a trespasser demolishes the building and replaces it with a structure that is merely a substitute.
material_facts: The respondents’ family had obtained the site from the appellants’ ancestors and built residential buildings on it.
The respondents temporarily left the village for safety during communal disturbances and returned when conditions improved.
The appellants unlawfully entered the site, demolished the respondents’ buildings and erected a cow-shed in their place.
The Court was not satisfied that the cow-shed was worth more than the demolished buildings and treated the new structure as a substitute for them.
The appellants refused to return possession, and the respondents’ possession claim was pending when vesting occurred.
issues.conclusion: The respondents had not abandoned their buildings; they were entitled to recover the site and the replacement building, which they owned and lawfully held at the time of vesting.
issues.legal_principle: A temporary departure for safety does not, without more, amount to abandonment. The trespassers’ demolition and replacement construction did not enhance their rights under the Transfer of Property Act. On the facts and equitable considerations, the respondents remained owners of the substituted building and were entitled to recover it. The Court left open the broader question whether a landowner may recover land together with a building erected on it by a stranger.

predicates.occupants_abandoned_building: The lawful occupants voluntarily gave up their building.

issues.definition: When lawful occupants temporarily leave without abandoning their building and a trespasser demolishes it and erects a replacement not shown to be more valuable, the prior lawful occupants own and may recover the replacement.

issues.legal_issue: Estate vesting and the deemed settlement of specified rights in buildings are legally separate transactions.
material_facts: The statutory scheme provided that notified estates vested in the State free from encumbrances and separately provided for deemed settlement of certain rights concerning specified lands or buildings.
The dispute concerned whether rights concerning a building under the settlement provision meant that the relevant interests had not vested in the State.
issues.conclusion: The estate first vests in the State absolutely and free from encumbrances; the deemed settlement of specified rights follows as a separate legal transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 6 and 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, must be read as providing for vesting followed by deemed settlement, even though the events occur simultaneously in fact. The Court relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank Ltd. and Shivashankar Prasad Shah v. Vaikunth Nath Singh, which concerned comparable statutory schemes.

predicates.estate_vests_under_scheme: The scheme provides that the estate vests in the State.
predicates.scheme_separately_settles_specified_prop: The scheme separately provides for settlement of specified rights concerning property within the estate.

issues.definition: When a land-reform scheme provides for both estate vesting and settlement of specified property rights, vesting and deemed settlement are separate transactions.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court bench that disagrees with a decision of a co-ordinate bench must refer the question to a larger bench rather than decline to follow that decision.
material_facts: A High Court Division Bench declined to follow an earlier decision of another Division Bench of co-ordinate jurisdiction.
The disagreement concerned the meaning of a statutory term, and the later bench did not refer the issue to a larger bench.
issues.conclusion: Judicial propriety requires a bench unable to agree with a decision of a co-ordinate bench to refer the question to a larger bench.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that judicial propriety requires referral to a larger bench when a High Court bench cannot agree with a decision of a co-ordinate bench; otherwise, conflicting decisions undermine public respect for the High Court and make the work of subordinate courts difficult.

predicates.high_court_bench_conflict_case: The case concerns disagreement between benches of the same High Court.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees_with_coordinate_be: A later bench cannot agree with a decision made by a bench of co-ordinate jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a later High Court bench disagrees with a decision of a co-ordinate bench, it should refer the question to a larger bench.
